text: This is the final chapter of the course, and it's one continuous capstone across three lessons. You're going to design, build, and review one real Script Include class, pulling together everything from JavaScript fundamentals through GlideRecord, GlideAjax, and debugging. This lesson is the kickoff: defining what the class needs to do, before writing any real implementation.

Here's the scenario. Picture your team's instance six months in. One Business Rule on incident checks whether the assigned user is in the Network group. A different Business Rule on change request does the same check, written slightly differently by someone else. Several scripts format a due date for display, each getting a slightly different result. Other scripts read a reference field's display value - some defensively check it's not empty first, some don't, and occasionally one throws an error in production. None of this is hard logic. The problem is duplication and drift, not difficulty.

Before implementing anything, a senior developer plans the public method signatures first - what goes in, what comes out. This capstone builds one Script Include, named TaskUtils, with three planned methods. isUserInGroup takes a user ID and a group name and returns true or false. formatDueDate takes a GlideDateTime object, not a raw string, and returns a display-ready string. getReferenceDisplayValue takes a GlideRecord and a field name and returns a string, safely.

Here's the empty shell this capstone starts from, using the same Class.create pattern Chapter 4 used for your first Script Include. Each of the three methods is a stub right now - a signature with no working code inside it yet. Notice the type property at the bottom, set to the string TaskUtils. That's required on every Script Include built this way - it's how ServiceNow's internal class system identifies it.

Here's the one design decision that matters most heading into Lesson 31. Of these three methods, only isUserInGroup might realistically be called from a Client Script - checking group membership before showing a UI message. The other two are naturally server-side helpers, called from Business Rules that already have a GlideRecord or GlideDateTime object in hand. That means TaskUtils needs to support plain server-side calls and one client-callable entry point, at the same time, in the same class.

Three stubs, one plan, one open design question about client-callable access. Next up: Lesson 31 turns every one of these stubs into real, working code, including the GlideAjax bridge that isUserInGroup needs.
